      Pick at least one server above to edit its System Configuration.

      [System]
      Copies Limit_DC_Max_IO_101625.run to /home/etdev and runs it to cap max_ninputs and max_nsdioutputs at each server’s ninputs and nsdioutputs below (16 max). SMPTE 2110 servers and Content Managers get neither.
      ⚠ video_codec = jpegxs (baseline or a server override) — those packages will also install the JPEG-XS license (binds to the target server's own /etc/machine-id at install time).
      features.conf
      toggle true / false per flag
      /etc/timezone
      also relinks /etc/localtime
      Services run on the target at install
      turn off firewall

      Runs ufw disable, then systemctl disable dcsfirewall.service so it stays off.

      mask timemaster (SDI systems)

      Runs systemctl mask timemaster on servers where input and output are both SDI. SMPTE 2110 servers are always skipped.

      SMB users Samba logins added at install
      add SMB users

      Each user: creates the Linux user if it isn’t there (no home, no login shell), then runs smbpasswd -a and smbpasswd -e. Keep guest access on makes sure map to guest = Bad User is set in [global] of /etc/samba/smb.conf (backed up to /home/etdev first) and reloads Samba without dropping connections, so guest shares keep working once named users exist. Skipped on servers without Samba. Passwords are written into each .efp and saved with the project.

      render_delay.json
      written to /etc/default/render_delay.json
      Export formats created through the DreamCatcher API at install
      create these export formats on the cluster

      Formats and profiles are shared across the cluster, so only one server’s .efp creates them: the first Content Manager, or the first server when there isn’t one.
      That installer writes /home/etdev/dc_export_formats.json and dc_export_formats.py, then logs in to the local JSON-RPC API (port 5001) and runs create_export_format, or update_export_format when a format with the same name already exists, so running it again is safe. With an export profile, it also runs create_export_profile (or update_export_profile) pointing at the new format, with the audio layout set to the first one ticked. If DCS isn’t up it waits about a minute, then skips; run the script in /home/etdev again later.

      Starts from Brandon's confirmed baseline. Uncheck anything you don't want touched, edit any value, then build your own EFP. Unchecked settings are left completely alone on the target server.

      Connectors
      Key is the connector's category address (for example 7000 or 9001) from persistence_key_mapping, not an arbitrary index. Each Input or Output group counts up from its first row when Sequential is ticked: video and anc step the last octet per input, audio steps the third octet per input and the last octet per audio stream (.1, .2, …). Unused connectors stay in the output as zeroed entries (ip: 0), so leave the IP blank to get that placeholder.

      One file to upload — every config applied
      

        
      
          Builds one file for the drop-and-install page. It updates the DreamCatcher signal routing and the
          Matrox network settings on the same server, using whatever's set on the Node config and Streams & Connectors pages, plus the DC routes file if
          you've loaded one. The old versions of every file touched are saved automatically first, so nothing
          is lost if something needs to be undone.
        
      
        
      
          Builds a single installer that writes the DreamCatcher persistence file (Streams & Connectors page), then applies the
          Matrox node config settings from the Node config page — in the mode currently
          selected there (find-on-server or uploaded file) — and, if one's loaded, deploys the DC routes
          file to /etc/dc-routes.json. Each part is backed up before being overwritten, and each
          part's success or failure is reported separately in the install log below.

            Deploy a patch. Drop in a .deb and get an .efp that does what you would do by hand:
              copies it into a folder on the server and runs sudo dpkg -i on it. This is its own package, separate from the base config and Matrox ones.

            1. Copies the .deb into the folder above, keeping its file name (it stays there afterwards).
              2. 
                
            2. Runs dpkg -i on that copy, with --force-confdef --force-confold so a changed config file can never stall the installer on a prompt (local edits are kept).
              3. 
                
            3. Checks dpkg now reports that exact package name and version as installed, and fails the install if not.
              4. 
              
            
              
            Dependencies must already be on the server, as with a manual dpkg -i. If any are missing, dpkg's list and the package state are written to the install log. The package name and version are read from the .deb itself on the server at install time.
